fetched_contents.text: Observations and simulations of immersion freezing INPs and their impact on cloud properties over the rain shadow region of India Highlights * • Immersion-freezing INP (Ice nucleating particle) measurements over India's rain shadow region are presented. * • A new empirical parameterization for immersion-freezing INPs is proposed. * • The impact of INP parameterization on cloud properties depends strongly on secondary ice production. Abstract Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) play a critical role in cloud microphysics, influencing precipitation efficiency and cloud lifetime. This study presents measurements of immersion-freezing INPs over the rain-shadow region of India, with immersion freezing and condensation freezing considered as a single mode. INP concentrations ranged from 2 to 12 L−1 between −15 °C to −35 °C. At −40 °C, which is representative of homogeneous freezing conditions, the ice crystal concentration reaches ∼800 L−1. Ice nucleation activity was further characterized through parameters such as ice fraction and active surface site density. These parameters, as functions of temperature and ice supersaturation, provide valuable constraints for representing mixed-phase cloud processes in weather and climate models. Observed INP concentrations showed weak sensitivity to coarse-mode aerosol number concentrations, in which positive correlations with aerosols are emerging only below −25 °C. An empirical INP–temperature parameterization was developed from observations and evaluated within the Weather Research & Forecasting model, alongside two commonly used immersion-freezing schemes. Simulations of mixed-phase monsoon clouds demonstrated that cloud properties such as cloud top temperature, supercooled liquid water content, ice content, and water paths are sensitive to the chosen INP parameterization, particularly in the absence of secondary ice production (SIP). Inclusion of SIP mechanisms reduced this sensitivity, as SIP-generated ice particles compensated for variations induced by heterogeneous nucleation. Minimal changes in surface precipitation were observed, likely due to dominant homogeneous freezing at upper cloud levels. Keywords Ice nucleating particles (INPs) ; Secondary ice production (SIP) ; SPIN ; Ice nucleation ; Immersion freezing ; CAIPEEX Introduction Ice particles in Earth's atmosphere play a central role in regulating precipitation processes and radiative transfer, thereby exerting a strong influence on the global hydrological cycle and climate system. In natural clouds, ice forms through primary and secondary ice production (SIP) mechanisms. The primary ice production occurs via homogeneous nucleation with spontaneous freezing of droplets below −38 °C and heterogeneous nucleation, where insoluble aerosol particles act as ice-nucleating particles (INPs) at warmer subzero temperatures (Pruppacher and Klett, 1997; Kanji et al., 2017). Only a small fraction of aerosols (≈1 in 105–106) serve as INPs (DeMott et al., 2003; Murray et al., 2012). SIP generates additional ice crystals from preexisting ones formed by primary ice production (Korolev et al., 2013; Korolev and Leisner, 2020). Unlike homogeneous nucleation, heterogeneous nucleation strongly depends on aerosol surface properties, making it difficult to represent in models. Heterogeneous ice nucleation occurs through four modes: immersion freezing, condensation freezing, contact freezing, and deposition nucleation (Vali, 1985; Vali et al., 2015; Kanji et al., 2017; DeMott et al., 2011). Immersion freezing is widely regarded as the key mechanism for mixed phase clouds (Ansmann et al., 2008; de Boer et al., 2011; Westbrook and Illingworth, 2013). Condensation freezing occurs when water condenses on INPs under near-saturated conditions and subsequently freezes, while contact freezing involves the collision of supercooled droplets with INPs. However, it should be noted that the distinction between condensation and immersion freezing is highly uncertain (Vali et al., 2015) and these two modes usually assumed as a single mode. Deposition nucleation, which bypasses the liquid phase by direct vapor deposition onto INPs at ice-supersaturated conditions, is thought to be minor in mixed-phase clouds but relevant in cirrus (Ansmann et al., 2008; Cziczo et al., 2003). Numerous studies have examined their physicochemical properties, sources, and mechanisms of ice nucleating activity (Kanji et al., 2017; Hoose and Möhler, 2012; Welti et al., 2009; Prenni et al., 2012; Gong et al., 2022; Knopf et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). INPs play a critical role in initiating the formation of the ice phase in clouds, thereby influencing the Earth's radiative balance and precipitation patterns (Lohmann and Feichter, 2005; Kanji et al., 2017; Burrows et al., 2022). Despite growing scientific attention, the sources, concentrations, and regional variability of INPs remain inadequately characterized in many parts of the world. INPs originate from diverse sources including desert dust, anthropogenic emissions, marine aerosols, and biological particles (Huang et al., 2021). Mineral dust aerosols serve as highly efficient INPs in the troposphere, especially at colder temperatures where heterogeneous ice nucleation becomes more active (Murray et al., 2012; Hoose and Möhler, 2012). Aerosols from biomass burning and fly ash also contribute to atmospheric INP populations (Prenni et al., 2012; McCluskey et al., 2014; Umo et al., 2015). Although generally less efficient than mineral dust, these aerosols can still facilitate ice nucleation. Biogenic aerosols, including primary biological particles such as bacteria, pollen, fungal spores, and their fragments, were first identified in the 1970s as important sources of INPs (Vali and Schnell, 2024; Schnell and Vali, 2024). Submission received: 20 June 2017 / Revised: 19 July 2017 / Accepted: 20 July 2017 / Published: 29 July 2017 Abstract There has been increasing interest in ice nucleation research in the last decade. To identify important gaps in our knowledge of ice nucleation processes and their impacts, two international workshops on ice nucleation were held in Vienna, Austria in 2015 and 2016. Experts from these workshops identified the following research needs: (1) uncovering the molecular identity of active sites for ice nucleation; (2) the importance of modeling for the understanding of heterogeneous ice nucleation; (3) identifying and quantifying contributions of biological ice nuclei from natural and managed environments; (4) examining the role of aging in ice nuclei; (5) conducting targeted sampling campaigns in clouds; and (6) designing lab and field experiments to increase our understanding of the role of ice-nucleating particles in the atmosphere. Interdisciplinary teams of scientists should work together to establish and maintain a common, unified language for ice nucleation research. A number of commercial applications benefit from ice nucleation research, including the production of artificial snow, the freezing and preservation of water-containing food products, and the potential modulation of weather. Additional work is needed to increase our understanding of ice nucleation processes and potential impacts on precipitation, water availability, climate change, crop health, and feedback cycles. 1. Background and Motivation The formation of ice in clouds occurs by homogeneous and heterogeneous ice nucleation [1]. Droplets in clouds nucleate on aerosol particles, some of which freeze to form ice crystals. A variety of ice-nucleating particles have been identified in clouds and implicated in precipitation, including soot, mineral dust, pollen, bacteria, and fungi [2,3]. There has been a resurgence in ice nucleation research within the last decade [4], largely because of the pressing need to understand the impact of aerosols on precipitation and climate. A recent AMS monograph on the topic has produced reviews in 11 chapters, covering topics including cirrus and contrail ice, ice fog, mixed-phase clouds, formation of precipitation, secondary ice production, and measurement methods [5]. In addition to atmospheric issues, there are a number of important commercial applications for ice nucleation research, including the production of artificial snow [6], the freezing and preservation of water-containing food products [7], the freeze protection of infrastructure [8], and the potential modulation of weather [9]. Many of these fields need new research to fill important gaps in fundamental knowledge of ice nucleation processes and their impacts. Here, we identify and discuss six major research needs and unanswered research questions in atmospheric ice nucleation research, many of which have received only cursory attention in the past. The major research topics in need of further work came out of the two international workshops held in Vienna in 2015 and 2016, and are briefly outlined in Section 2 through 7 of this manuscript. The workshops were held 11–12 April, 2015 and 16–17 April, 2016 at the Italian Cultural Institute in Vienna, Austria. Meteoritic particles vary substantially in composition across meteorite classes, with the most primitive types preserving the most intact pre-atmospheric chemical inventory. Chondrites are especially notable for containing abundant indigenous organic material, and the evidence here states that “only the most primitive types of meteorite, the chondrites, contain abundant indigenous organic material” [N1-R1]. Carbonaceous chondrites are a subset of meteorites that originate from C-type asteroids and contain organic materials, including amino acids, nucleobases, and other organic compounds [N1-R3]. The majority of carbon in primitive chondrites is present as insoluble organic matter, which accounts for more than 50% of total organic carbon and is described as structurally complex aromatic material [N1-R2]. These findings support the idea that carbonaceous chondrites are richer in organic matter than other meteorite classes.

The mineralogical and elemental composition of meteoritic particles also includes silicates, oxides, sulfides, and volatiles. One source notes that chondritic meteorites contain hydrated Mg silicates, Fe3O4, and carbonate and sulfate compounds, with aggregate composition similar to solar matter [N1-R4]. Chondrites are described as stony, non-metallic meteorites that have not been modified by melting or differentiation of the parent body [N1-R5], which implies that their mineralogy reflects a relatively unaltered primordial composition. By contrast, the evidence does not provide a direct mineralogical breakdown for all meteorite types beyond chondrites and carbonaceous chondrites, so the strongest supported statement is that these classes differ in their preservation of organics, while silicates and secondary minerals like carbonates/sulfates appear common in chondrites.

The composition differs most clearly between chondrites, carbonaceous chondrites, and other meteorite types. Chondrites are the most primitive and richest in indigenous organic matter [N1-R1], whereas carbonaceous chondrites are a specialized class of chondrite that contains even more organic material, including amino acids and nucleobases [N1-R3]. The other meteorite types in the evidence are not fully characterized, but the contrast is clear: chondrites preserve pre-atmospheric organics, carbonaceous chondrites amplify that organic signature, and the evidence does not explicitly describe a third class as equally rich in organics. The main compositional distinction is therefore between preserved organics and the broader group of less primitive meteorites, with carbonaceous chondrites as a more extreme example of organic enrichment [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

The evidence for meteoritic particles as ice-nucleating particles is primarily indirect and comparative, rather than a direct demonstration of their role as INPs. The provided material does not include a direct experimental study on meteoritic particles themselves, but it does provide a broad experimental framework for measuring ice-nucleating activity and comparing aerosol types. One key source describes PINE as an instrument designed to study ice nucleation processes and measure INP concentrations across the full tropospheric temperature range, showing agreement with established cloud chambers for homogeneous freezing of pure water droplets and immersion freezing under controlled conditions [N5-F3]. Another source notes that ice nucleation measurements can be done through immersion freezing at temperatures greater than −33 °C, with temperature, ambient humidity/ice supersaturation, and freezing mode strongly affecting the rate and onset of freezing [N7-R2]. These materials establish that INP activity is typically quantified using temperature-dependent activation measurements and that immersion freezing is a central mode of study [N5-F3][N7-R2].

The evidence also shows how experimental activation efficiencies are compared across aerosol types. A recent review states that INP concentrations vary strongly with temperature and that different aerosol types dominate the INP population at specific temperatures [N6-F1]. It also notes that mineral dust is among the most important INP sources and that INP activity is highly sensitive to particle type [N6-F1]. Although the provided evidence does not explicitly compare meteoritic particles with mineral or biological INPs in a direct study, it does support the general framework for such comparisons: INP activity is measured using empirical parameterizations, INP–temperature relationships, and direct sampling methods that expose particles to desired supersaturation and temperature conditions [N7-R4][N7-R2].
